name: Bubble Tea
summary: A Go framework from Charm for terminal apps built on the Elm Architecture: one model holds the state, Update turns messages into a new model, and View describes the screen.
intro: A Bubble Tea program is a model plus three methods. `Init` returns an optional first command. `Update` receives a message (a key press, a mouse click, a window resize, a timer tick, a server response), returns the updated model and optionally a command. `View` turns the model into a `tea.View`, and the runtime redraws after every update, so the app has no redrawing logic of its own. Commands (`tea.Cmd`) are functions that do I/O; the runtime runs each one in its own goroutine and feeds the message it returns back into `Update`. `tea.Batch` runs several at once with no ordering guarantees, `tea.Sequence` one after another.

Version 2, released in February 2026, made the view declarative: instead of commands such as `tea.EnterAltScreen`, `View` sets fields like `AltScreen`, `MouseMode` and the window title, and the runtime applies them. Its “Cursed Renderer”, modeled on the ncurses rendering algorithm, redraws at most 60 times a second by default (configurable up to 120); Charm says it cuts bandwidth by orders of magnitude for apps served over SSH with its Wish library. It reads the Kitty keyboard protocol where the terminal supports it, so apps can bind keys like shift+enter and see key releases, and it downsamples colors to what the terminal can show. Apps can run full-window in the alternate screen or inline below the prompt.

Bubble Tea is the interaction layer of a set of Charm libraries: Bubbles provides components such as text inputs, viewports and spinners, and Lip Gloss handles styling and layout. Charmbracelet, Inc. is an active, venture-funded company: it shipped v2.1.0 in October 2026 and builds its own AI coding agent, Crush, on these libraries.
strengths: One model and one Update function make state changes predictable and easy to test: every change comes from a message
Concurrency without shared state: commands run in goroutines and report back as messages, so I/O never blocks the UI
A family of libraries (Bubbles components, Lip Gloss styling, Wish for SSH apps) and, per its README, more than 18,000 applications built on it, including tools from AWS, NVIDIA and Microsoft Azure
v2 handles modern terminal features for you: keyboard enhancements, color downsampling, synchronized rendering and clipboard transfer over SSH
limits: v2 broke the API: the import path moved to `charm.land/bubbletea/v2`, `View` returns a `tea.View` instead of a string, and key and mouse messages were split into new types, so v1 code needs the upgrade guide
The app owns stdin and stdout, so you can’t print-debug: logs go to a file (`tea.LogToFile`) and Delve must run in headless mode
Commands started with `tea.Batch` run concurrently with no ordering guarantees, so their messages can arrive in any order; use `tea.Sequence` when order matters
Richer key handling only works in terminals that support progressive keyboard enhancement (Ghostty, Kitty, WezTerm, iTerm2 and others); apps need fallbacks elsewhere

snippet.title: A countdown that ticks with a command (Bubble Tea v2)
source: // A command: the runtime runs it in a goroutine and sends its result to Update.
return tea.Tick(time.Second, func(t time.Time) tea.Msg { return tickMsg(t) })
func (m model) Init() tea.Cmd { return tick() }
return tea.NewView(fmt.Sprintf("Quitting in %d seconds. Press q to quit now.\n", m.left))

story: Charm started in 2019 as a group of friends from consumer tech (Apple, Last.fm, TweetDeck) who wanted to bring modern product design to the command line. Their first projects, Glow and Glamour, styled Markdown in the terminal, but they also needed a way to build interactive interfaces. Christian Rocha, who came from Haskell and Elm, wanted to write stateful text interfaces without thinking about rendering, and found nothing in the Go ecosystem that did it, so the team built Bubble Tea on the Elm Architecture. Its first tagged release, v0.1.0, came out in April 2020.

Bubble Tea grew with its sister libraries, Bubbles and Lip Gloss, and with Charm’s own tools built on them, such as Glow. By November 2023, when Charm raised $6 million in a round led by Gradient, Google’s AI-focused fund, it powered more than 4,000 apps. Charm tagged v1.0.0 in August 2024 as an “honorary release” to mark the API as stable.

When AI coding agents moved into the terminal, Charm decided the libraries had to carry more weight. Bubble Tea v2, released with Lip Gloss and Bubbles v2 on 23 February 2026, brought the new Cursed Renderer, richer keyboard input and a declarative view; the v2 branches had run Charm’s coding agent Crush in production for months first. Charm says it had never pushed a breaking change before v2.

choices.why: A single model updated only by messages lets developers build stateful, animated interfaces without managing redraws, the experience Charm’s founders knew from building browser UIs in Elm.
All I/O goes through `tea.Cmd` functions that the runtime runs concurrently and turns into messages, so many asynchronous operations stay simple and the model is only touched in `Update`.

choices.choice: Inline mode as a first-class use case, compiled to native code
choices.why: Charm wanted interfaces that can appear inline in a normal terminal session, not only full-screen apps, and sees speed as one of the terminal’s main advantages, locally and over SSH.

choices.choice: A declarative view and one owner of terminal I/O in v2
choices.why: In v1, Bubble Tea and Lip Gloss could fight over the terminal (one reading keys, the other querying the background color), and terminal modes were toggled with commands. In v2 Bubble Tea owns all I/O and the view simply declares what it wants.
